title: Teacher training in the age of AI: Impact on AI Literacy and Teachers' Attitudes
extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether an online professional development program can improve in-service teachers’ AI literacy, their attitudes toward AI, and their self-reported willingness to use AI in teaching. The authors position the study as a response to the rapid spread of generative AI in education and the need for teachers to develop both conceptual understanding and practical confidence, rather than simply being aware of AI in the abstract.

The intervention was a four-week certificate course offered by the digital professional development platform fobizz, titled “Artificial Intelligence in Everyday School and Classroom Practice.” The course combined a kickoff webinar, self-paced learning modules, optional supplementary webinars and workshops, and a project phase in which participants created an AI-supported lesson plan using tools such as the fobizz AI Assistant. The sample consisted of German in-service teachers from a range of school types, with some participants also coming from adult education, higher education, and school administration. Outcomes were measured with pre-post questionnaires assessing AI literacy and attitudes toward AI, including self-reported current use, intended classroom integration, perceived preparedness, and beliefs about opportunities and risks.

The findings show statistically significant gains in overall AI literacy and in most competency domains, along with large positive shifts in self-reported use of AI in daily life and teaching practice, and in feeling prepared to integrate AI into lessons. The authors conclude that structured training can improve teachers’ AI-related knowledge, confidence, and willingness to use AI educationally. However, they also note that post-training knowledge remained incomplete, that the sample was self-selected, and that the study did not assess long-term sustainability or whether teachers actually implemented AI practices beyond the immediate post-test.

identified_tools.name: fobizz AI Assistant
identified_tools.description: A digital AI assistant offered within the fobizz professional development platform for generating and supporting classroom materials and lesson planning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by participating teachers during the training course to develop an AI-supported lesson plan and to practice pedagogically reflective AI use in classroom contexts.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers in the training program showed increased self-reported use of AI tools for lesson planning and teaching materials after the intervention. The paper reports that agreement increased significantly for "I use AI to help create my lessons and teaching materials" (pre M=1.27, post M=2.35, p<0.001, d=1.32; n=436) and for "I feel well-prepared to integrate AI technologies into my teaching" (pre M=1.03, post M=2.28, p<0.001, d=1.65; n=436).
findings.measure: Self-reported use of AI for lesson creation and perceived preparedness to integrate AI into teaching

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI generative AI chatbot based on large language models used for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in the core training module "ChatGPT & fobizz AI in Your Classroom" and discussed as a generative AI tool teachers should learn to use in educational practice.

findings.finding_summary: After the training, teachers reported significantly higher current and intended use of AI in daily and educational practice. Items increased for regular AI use in daily life (pre M=1.37, post M=2.28, p<0.001, d=1.07; n=436), use for lesson/material creation (pre M=1.27, post M=2.35, p<0.001, d=1.32; n=436), use for assessments/grading (pre M=0.41, post M=1.04, p<0.001, d=0.67; n=436), and imagining AI integration into teaching (pre M=2.45, post M=2.72, p<0.001, d=0.49; n=436).
findings.measure: Self-reported AI use, intended integration, and preparedness for teaching

findings.finding_summary: The training also increased critical beliefs about AI risks while increasing belief in AI's instructional value. Agreement that "AI in schools is more of a threat than an opportunity" rose slightly (pre M=0.98, post M=1.37, p<0.001, d=0.42; n=436), and concern that "AI will replace teachers in the future" also increased slightly (pre M=0.45, post M=0.67, p<0.001, d=0.25; n=436), but belief that AI offers an opportunity to support students increased as well (pre M=2.39, post M=2.67, p<0.001, d=0.50; n=436).
findings.measure: Self-reported beliefs about AI opportunities and risks in education

quality_tier_rationale: This is a pre-post intervention study with self-reported outcomes, not a randomized controlled trial. It provides useful evidence on teacher attitudes and reported use, but the design limits causal inference and the paper does not isolate effects of a single tool.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect sizes for several self-reported outcomes are medium to very large (e.g., d=1.32 and d=1.65). Even though the evidence is self-reported, the magnitude of change suggests substantial perceived impact.
